title: AnyBlock JSON property dictionary
description: One properties.json at the root of a bundle names every property the bundle's objects use — the dictionary (§2f). It is a sibling of index.json, not a section inside it: an index says where things are, a dictionary says what they mean. A bundle carries no property document at all (§15 #23): this file is where every property something references is stated — replacing the ~9,500 documents per account (kind "property") that restated the bundled table field for field (98% of installed copies are identical to it), and the rest besides — and it is what lets a third-party reader interpret a backup WITHOUT shipping the bundled table: every entry carries its format, so a date is a date and an option name is an option name even to a reader that has never seen Anytype.

$schema.description: Which of the format's three grammars this document follows — an object document, a bundle index, or a property dictionary. OPTIONAL and DECORATIVE for validity: `formatVersion` alone gates the format, so a stale or invented URL here never makes a document invalid. What it does do is DISPATCH: a reader handed a file with no filename to go by uses this to pick the grammar, matching on the trailing `object|index|properties.schema.json` and ignoring the version segment. Without it a reader falls back to the document's shape, which can only tell the grammars apart when the document happens to carry a member unique to one. Every document this format writes carries it, and a hand-written one is easier for a reader to place if it does too.

properties.description: One propertyDefinition per property the bundle's objects actually REFERENCE — used-only, not everything the space holds: a space installs a median 125 bundled properties and uses 57, and the 68 nothing touches buy a reader nothing (the restore reinstalls the bundled table anyway). A property nothing references is not exported at all — no document (a bundle carries none, §15 #23), no entry: nothing names the key, so there is no value to explain and no format to look up. This is the dictionary's ONE list (§15 #24): a bundled property the bundle carries is an entry here like any other, and every entry states the COMPLETE definition — name, format, description, object types, include-time on a date, max count on a format that can hold more than one value, readonly, default value, options, the entry's own flags — whatever the property has and its format leaves room for, whether the key is bundled or space-minted, whether the space's copy matched the shipped table or not (§15 #25). There is no reduced entry that leaves a reader to fill the rest from its own table, and no reader needs the table to interpret the file. A reader tells a bundled key from a space-minted one by looking the stored key up in its own shipped table, the lookup every §3 slot runs, never by a flag on the entry; `bundled_diverged` is not that flag — it says a bundled key's copy had DIVERGED from the table at export time, and its absence says nothing about bundled-ness. Keys are CANONICAL SPELLINGS: the display name from the shipped table for a bundled key, the stored key verbatim for a space-minted one — a pure function of the key, because this file carries no legend. The reader flow is object → spelling → (1) the document's property_internal_keys legend, (2) a verbatim match against a dictionary key, (3) the shipped name table over the dictionary's own keys, with the forgiving fold behind it for near-misses and pre-v0.48 derived-slug spellings. Step 3 carries most value slots, because §3 writes a legend line only for a spelling the bundled table does not bind. Look up, never transform: the name and the key say different words (`Creation date` / `createdDate`). No folder convention, no scanning (§2f).

dictionaryEntry.description: One dictionary entry: a propertyDefinition (§2e), referenced rather than restated. Its `property` is the entry's spelling: the display name for a bundled property (`Due date`), the stored key verbatim for a space-minted one — a bson id like `6a32d4856761631534b22f85`, from which nothing must ever be derived. Its `internal_key` is the stored key itself, written by export for fidelity and never required from an author. This is the third of the shape's three homes, beside a type document's property-definition entry and a property document's property_settings — and the only one a bundle this format's composer writes (§15 #23), which is why its three owned members — `uninstalled`, `hidden` and `bundled_diverged` — carry what a property document used to, and what only the export could know. The layer narrows `object_types` to a real array (only a property document's STORED value can hold a null; a dictionary describes, it does not mirror a store slot) and requires `format`, because self-sufficiency is the constraint that shapes the dictionary: an entry without a format is readable only by a reader shipping the same bundled vocabulary, which is exactly the dependence the dictionary exists to end. An entry must identify the property it declares: state a `property` (the spelling), or an `internal_key` (the stored id), or a `name` the spelling is derived from. A NAME ALONE IS ENOUGH — `{"name": "Cooking Time", "format": "number"}` declares a property spelled `Cooking Time`. Prefer `property` or `name` when authoring: `internal_key` is an id the app mints, an author has no space to draw one from, and inventing one is never right — when a custom property states none, the import wiring mints a fresh internal key exactly as the app does when a user creates one. A derived spelling runs through the same resolution as a written one, so a property named "Due Date" folds onto the bundled `dueDate` instead of minting a lookalike beside it.

name.description: When name supplies the property identity, readers NFC-normalize it before applying the 128-character writable-key bound. Standard JSON Schema cannot count characters after normalization, so this schema enforces the expressible non-empty/control-free part and semantic readers enforce the normalized maximum.

object_types.description: objects/files only: the types the property may point at, in priority order, each written as the type's derived id `type-<internal_key>` (§9); a display name or the legacy `ot-<key>` is accepted on input.

uninstalled.description: The user REMOVED this property from the space, and the bundle carries it for backup fidelity rather than as a document (§2f, §15 #22). Export writes `true` only; absent is the same statement as `false`, and an author never writes it — there is nothing to uninstall in a bundle that has not been installed. A reader MAY recreate the property with its removal mark set, or skip it: a removed property appears in no listing either way, so both restores look the same, and the entry still says what a value stored under the key means. What a reader MUST NOT do is install it as a live property. The flag is the whole statement of the removal (§15 #24): the dictionary keeps no list of installed keys for it to contradict. A member of the dictionary entry only: on a type's property_definitions entry or a property document's property_settings it would describe nothing, and both homes refuse it, as this one refuses `section`.

hidden.description: The store HIDES this property from every listing (its stored `isHidden`), and a bundle carries no property document to say so (§2f, §15 #23), so the entry does. Export writes `true` only; absent is the same statement as `false`, and an author never writes it — a property is declared to be used, and hiding one is a store fact the export records, like `internal_key`. A reader that recreates the property sets the mark; a reader that only interprets values ignores it. Distinct from a type declaration's `section`, which says where a property sits on ONE type: `hidden` says whether the property is shown at all. A member of the dictionary entry only, on the same footing as `uninstalled`: the shape's other two homes refuse it.

bundled_diverged.description: The space's copy of a BUNDLED property — a key the shipped table names — had DIVERGED from that table when the bundle was written (§2f, §15 #25): a rename, a changed description or hidden bit, any definition member. The entry states the user's version, complete, like every entry; this member says that version is the user's and not the table's, so a reader restoring the key takes the entry over its own table. It is written because it is NOT derivable: a reader could diff the entry against its table today, but the shipped table moves between app versions — once Anytype renames a bundled property, a later reader cannot tell whether the user renamed it or the table did. The verdict is knowable only at export time, and this records it. Export writes `true` only, and only for a key in the writer's shipped table whose copy the identity check refused; absent means EITHER "not a bundled property" OR "bundled and not diverged", and the reader separates those with the table lookup it already runs for every key (§15 #24) — this is not a `bundled` flag. Reader behaviour: key in the reader's table and no flag → install the fresh bundled property, accepting any newer name the table has; key in the table with `bundled_diverged: true` → the user's version wins, create or update from the entry; key not in the reader's table → create from the entry, flag or no flag. An author never writes it — there is no space whose copy could have diverged. A member of the dictionary entry only, on the same footing as `uninstalled` and `hidden`: the shape's other two homes refuse it.
